redditSourcedNotes: Nothing in this file is reddit-sourced. The research stage executed no searches at all (its search budget was already exhausted), so the queries it listed never ran and have been replaced here by the five WebSearch calls the verify stage actually ran. Every source URL attached below appeared in one of those five results; spots with an empty sources array were verified from the reviewer's own knowledge of Istanbul, conservatively, and say so in verifyNote. Wikipedia titles were kept only where a search result showed the en.wikipedia.org URL (Rami Library, Hasanpaşa Gasworks) or where the reviewer is highly confident the article exists for exactly this place (Yıldız Park, Emirgan Park, Belgrad Forest, Little Hagia Sophia, Süleymaniye Mosque); 'Atatürk Library' was set to null because the search surfaced only Wikidata and Turkish Wikipedia entries. A future pass with search budget should re-run the reddit-first query set and attach local-opinion sources.

spots.name: Moda Sahil Parkı
spots.blurb: The strip of park and rocky shoreline that wraps the Moda headland on the Asian side, where Kadıköy locals bring a thermos of tea, a beer or a book and sit on the rocks facing the old city. The sun goes down behind the minarets of the historic peninsula, and the shore fills with a spread-out crowd of couples, students and old men with fishing rods. It is popular but nobody is selling you anything, and there is usually a free patch of rock or grass.
spots.tips: Come 45 minutes before sunset and walk past the Moda pier toward the tip of the headland for the widest view; bring something to sit on, as the rocks get cold. The promenade lights stay on all night but the rocks themselves are unlit.

safety.note: Busy, well-lit promenade until well after midnight; the rocky shore below the path is unlit, so keep to the paths after dark.

spots.verifyNote: Well-known public shoreline park; verified from reviewer knowledge, no search spent. No exact-place English Wikipedia article (the Moda article covers the neighbourhood), so title left null.

spots.name: Fenerbahçe Parkı
spots.blurb: A tree-shaded seaside park on the small Fenerbahçe peninsula, with a 16th-century lighthouse at the tip, ferries sliding past toward the Princes' Islands and more cats than people on a weekday morning. Locals come to walk the loop path, sit on a bench under the pines and watch the boats in the marina. It has none of the bustle of central Kadıköy and suits a slow morning or a golden-hour stroll.
spots.tips: Enter from the Fenerbahçe pier end and walk out toward the lighthouse; the benches on the seaward southern side get the sunrise over the Marmara. Weekend afternoons draw families with picnic baskets, so go on a weekday for real quiet.

sources.label: Hürriyet: Fenerbahçe Parkı history and features
Nomadic Niko: Fenerbahçe neighbourhood and park
Mindtrip: Fenerbahçe Parkı, what to know before you go

safety.note: Main paths are lit and there is a marina next door; the tip of the peninsula is dim late at night, so keep to the inner path after 11pm.

spots.verifyNote: Existence, free entry and 24h access confirmed by search. Only a Turkish Wikipedia article exists; the English 'Fenerbahçe, Kadıköy' article is the neighbourhood, so title left null.

spots.name: Müze Gazhane
spots.blurb: A former 19th-century gasworks turned into a free public culture campus by the city in 2021, with brick gasometers, a public library, an open courtyard, exhibition halls and a couple of cafes. You can spend a rainy afternoon reading in the library, then drift into a free exhibition without anyone hurrying you. The crowd is neighbourhood families, students and people working on laptops rather than tourists.
spots.tips: The library has the best quiet desks; the outdoor courtyard between the gasometers is good for a coffee when it is dry. Check the site for closing days and event evenings, which can make the courtyard busy.

sources.label: Domus: Müze Gazhane, the gasworks museum powering Istanbul again
Istanbul Biennial (IKSV): Müze Gazhane venue page

safety.note: Staffed, enclosed site with security; the surrounding streets are busy residential Kadıköy.

spots.verifyNote: Confirmed by search; the English Wikipedia article for this exact site is 'Hasanpaşa Gasworks' (en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hasanpaşa_Gasworks), which is the museum's former name.

spots.name: Yıldız Parkı
spots.blurb: The old Ottoman palace grounds above Beşiktaş: a steep, wooded park with ponds, winding paths, huge plane trees and two 19th-century pavilions that now serve tea. Ten minutes uphill from the gate the traffic noise fades and you are among magnolias and rare trees. Locals come to walk the loops, read on a bench by the upper pond, or spread a blanket on the lawns.
spots.tips: Enter from the lower gate on Çırağan Caddesi and take the left-hand path uphill to the ponds for the quietest benches. Bring your own snacks; the pavilion cafes are pleasant but pricey.

safety.note: Gated park with staff at the entrances; paths are hilly and dim toward closing, so aim to leave before dark.

spots.verifyNote: Major public park; verified from reviewer knowledge, no search spent. 'Yıldız Park' kept as the English Wikipedia title on high confidence, not search-confirmed this session.

spots.name: Minoa Books & Coffee
spots.blurb: A bookshop-cafe in one of the restored Akaretler row houses, with a large English and Turkish selection and long tables and window seats where people settle in with a laptop or a paperback. Nobody moves you along after one coffee, and the low hum of readers is the right background noise. It sits on a quiet, tree-lined street a short walk uphill from the Beşiktaş waterfront.
spots.tips: Weekday mornings are the calmest; weekend afternoons fill with brunch crowds. The tables furthest from the counter are the quietest for work or reading.

safety.note: Busy, well-lit neighbourhood street; open late with plenty of foot traffic.

spots.verifyNote: Established bookshop-cafe on Süleyman Seba Caddesi in Akaretler; verified from reviewer knowledge, no search spent. Hours unconfirmed.

spots.name: Emirgan Korusu
spots.blurb: A large hillside grove on the European shore of the Bosphorus, with three pastel Ottoman pavilions serving tea, a pond, lawns and long shaded paths that climb to views over the strait. It is famous for its tulips in April, but outside those weeks it is a locals' park: joggers at dawn, families on the lawns and people reading under the trees. You can walk for an hour and rarely hear a car.
spots.tips: Avoid the April tulip festival weekends if you want quiet; any other month is calm. The upper terraces near the Pink Pavilion have the best Bosphorus views for a morning coffee.

safety.note: Gated, staffed park; paths are lit near the pavilions but dim on the upper trails after dark.

spots.verifyNote: Major public park; verified from reviewer knowledge, no search spent. 'Emirgan Park' kept as the English Wikipedia title on high confidence, not search-confirmed this session.

spots.name: Belgrad Ormanı
spots.blurb: The great oak and beech forest on the northern edge of the city, laced with old Ottoman aqueducts and reservoirs and a well-marked network of walking and running loops. On a weekday morning it is birdsong, joggers and the odd cyclist; on weekends city families spread out at the picnic clearings. It is the easiest way to get properly out of Istanbul without leaving it.
spots.tips: Take the bus or a taxi to the Bahçeköy entrance and follow the main loop of about 6 km around the Neşetsuyu reservoir; bring water and go early, as picnic spots fill by noon on weekends. Entry on foot is free; cars pay a small fee.

safety.note: No lighting and patchy phone signal off the main loop; go in daylight, stick to marked trails and take a friend if you head deep into the forest.

spots.verifyNote: Legitimate, managed public forest; caution kept for the unlit, remote trails. Verified from reviewer knowledge, no search spent. 'Belgrad Forest' kept as the English Wikipedia title on high confidence.

spots.name: Salacak Sahili
spots.blurb: The waterfront path south of Üsküdar pier that faces the Maiden's Tower, with the whole silhouette of the old city laid out across the water. Every evening Üsküdar locals come with tea, sunflower seeds and blankets to sit on the benches or the seawall and watch the sun drop behind the minarets. It stays lively and lit well into the night, and it costs nothing.
spots.tips: Arrive an hour before sunset for a bench near the Maiden's Tower boat landing; tea sellers wander the shore, or bring a thermos. The path continues south toward Harem if the main stretch is full.

safety.note: Busy, well-lit promenade until late; tea sellers and families around most of the night.

spots.verifyNote: Well-known public promenade; verified from reviewer knowledge, no search spent. The English 'Salacak' article is the neighbourhood, not the promenade, so title left null.

spots.name: Nevmekan Sahil
spots.blurb: A municipality-run library and cafe in a restored building on the Üsküdar waterfront beside the Şemsi Paşa Mosque, with high-ceilinged reading rooms, cheap tea and windows looking across the Bosphorus. Entry is free and it is used mostly by Üsküdar students and people working late; the domed halls are hushed and the cafe tables are relaxed. It is a good rain-day spot and one of the few calm places open late on the Asian shore.
spots.tips: Weeknights after 9pm are quietest; exam seasons fill the desks early. Bring headphones if you sit in the cafe section rather than the silent reading rooms, and step out to the seawall for a sunset break.

safety.note: Staffed public building on a busy, lit waterfront; Üsküdar pier and transport are two minutes away.

spots.verifyNote: Üsküdar Municipality's Nevmekan Sahil library-cafe; verified from reviewer knowledge, no search spent. Exact hours unconfirmed; no English Wikipedia article known.

spots.name: Nakkaştepe Millet Bahçesi
spots.blurb: A landscaped public garden on the Nakkaştepe hill above Kuzguncuk, with lawns, walking paths, picnic areas, a playground, cafes and tea gardens, and upper terraces that look straight at the Bosphorus Bridge and across to the European shore. Because it is uphill from the ferry piers, most visitors are neighbourhood residents walking the dog or watching the bridge lights come on. Weekday evenings are calm; Sunday afternoons bring families.
spots.tips: Walk up from Kuzguncuk pier through the village streets (about 15 steep minutes) or take a taxi to the top gate; head for the upper terrace facing the bridge at golden hour. A tea from the garden cafe is the cheapest way to sit with the view.

sources.label: Tripadvisor: Üsküdar Nakkaştepe Millet Bahçesi reviews
Cogito Istanbul: Nakkaştepe Millet Bahçesi, a panoramic park above the Bosphorus
Apex Travel Journal: 12 quiet sunset spots on the Bosphorus

safety.note: Lit paths and regular visitors until late; the hillside streets down to Kuzguncuk are quiet after midnight, so walk down with a friend or take a taxi.

spots.verifyNote: Existence in Kuzguncuk/Üsküdar and the bridge-facing terraces confirmed by search. Coordinates re-estimated to the hilltop next to Nakkaştepe cemetery but not confirmed by a map source, so left at low confidence; blurb rewritten to match what the sources describe (cafes, playground, picnic areas rather than an amphitheatre).

spots.name: Küçük Ayasofya Medrese Courtyard
spots.blurb: The cloister-like courtyard of the small medrese attached to the 6th-century Church of Sts Sergius and Bacchus, now a mosque, ten minutes downhill from the Blue Mosque and a world away from its crowds. The former students' cells around the courtyard hold craft workshops and a tea garden under a fig tree, and the arcades give shade or shelter from rain. You can sit with a tea for an hour and see maybe a dozen people.
spots.tips: Enter through the gate on Küçük Ayasofya Caddesi; the tea garden tables in the far corner of the courtyard are the quietest. Dress modestly if you step into the mosque itself; the courtyard is relaxed.

safety.note: Calm residential lane near the sea walls; well-frequented by day, quiet but fine in the evening.

spots.verifyNote: Mosque courtyard with tea garden and craft shops, publicly open; verified from reviewer knowledge, no search spent. 'Little Hagia Sophia' kept as the English Wikipedia title on high confidence (article covers the mosque and its complex).

spots.name: Süleymaniye Mosque Terrace
spots.blurb: The stone terrace and garden wall on the Golden Horn side of Sinan's great mosque, where the ground drops away to a view over Galata, the bridges and the mouth of the Bosphorus. Tourists come for the mosque; the terrace and the low walls along the cemetery garden are where Istanbul University students and neighbourhood elders sit with tea. At golden hour the light hits the Galata Tower straight on and the call to prayer rolls across the water.
spots.tips: Walk around the outside of the mosque to the north-east terrace behind the tombs; the tea gardens under the walls on Mimar Sinan Caddesi are good for a longer sit. Mornings are near-empty; the mosque courtyard closes to visitors during prayers.

safety.note: Well-lit and visited until late evening; the surrounding student streets thin out after 11pm.

spots.verifyNote: Famous landmark, but the outer terrace is a genuine free sit-and-look spot; verified from reviewer knowledge, no search spent. 'Süleymaniye Mosque' kept as the English Wikipedia title on high confidence.

spots.name: Atatürk Kitaplığı
spots.blurb: The city's public research library on Mete Caddesi at the edge of Gezi Park, a 1970s modernist building by Sedad Hakkı Eldem whose reading rooms have long run around the clock, free, with students still at their desks in the small hours. Big windows on the upper floors look out over the treetops toward the Bosphorus, and the hush is complete despite Taksim being two minutes away. It is a reliable place to sit and think at night in Istanbul.
spots.tips: Bring ID to register at the entrance; laptops are fine but the upper reading rooms are silent. Seats are scarce in exam months, so arrive before evening or come after midnight when the crowd thins.
spots.hours: 24h (confirm current schedule on the library site)

sources.label: IMM Atatürk Library: architecture and history
Daily Sabah: Istanbul's 24/7 Atatürk Library chosen as Turkey's best

safety.note: Staffed 24h with security at the door; Taksim Square and the metro are a short, lit walk away.

spots.verifyNote: Existence, location on Mete Caddesi and 24/7 service confirmed by search (official site, 2016 press). The search surfaced only a Wikidata item and the Turkish Wikipedia article, not an en.wikipedia.org URL, so the 'Atatürk Library' title was set to null per the strict photo rule.

spots.name: Rami Kütüphanesi
spots.blurb: A vast public library opened in January 2023 inside the restored 18th-century Rami Barracks, with a huge inner courtyard of lawns and trees, long reading galleries, a children's library, cafes and seating for some 4,200 readers, open around the clock and free. It sits in an unglamorous residential district well off any tourist route, so the crowd is neighbourhood students, retirees reading newspapers and families in the courtyard. Even when full it feels spacious and calm.
spots.tips: Take the bus or a taxi from Eyüp; the courtyard benches under the trees are the best outdoor spot and the upper galleries the quietest indoors. Register at the entrance with ID; food is only allowed in the cafe areas.

sources.label: Middle East Eye: Istanbul's Rami library, from army barracks to place of learning
World Cities Culture Forum: transforming Rami Barracks into Rami Library

safety.note: 24h staffed site with security; the surrounding streets are quiet late, so take a taxi or bus after midnight.

spots.verifyNote: Confirmed by search: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rami_Library exists for this exact library (opened 13 January 2023 in Rami Barracks, 4,200 seats).
